Biba op-art mini-dress

A long-sleeved jersey mini-dress from the London boutique Biba, printed with nested diamonds in brown and black.

Source
V&A: Mini-dress, T.159-1986
Creator
Biba (designer)
Made
1965
Style
Op art (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Mod, vibrating, murky
Evidence
Downloaded and inspected the V&A photograph of its copy, T.159-1986 (1040 × 1600 px), on a dress form against a blue backdrop, in a scratchpad. No image is stored.
Reviewed
28 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

The V&A catalogues the dress with the style “Op art” and says it “was produced during the short lived Op Art fashion trend of 1965”. A horizontal-stripe version was also made. V&A.

The V&A notes that “while true optical art was often stark white and black, other colourways were used”, and that Biba used a brown and black textile here. It quotes Barbara Hulanicki on prints that washed out to “faded grey Op-Art print dresses”. V&A.

Physical description: straight-cut mini-dress with a high neck and long sleeves, brown jersey with black op-art geometric print, back zip. V&A.

Observed

  • The print is a grid of concentric diamonds made of alternating brown and black bands of equal width.
  • Where four diamond centres meet, the bands turn into small checkerboards, and between them the bands form large X shapes.
  • The pattern covers the body, sleeves, and roll collar with no plain area.

Why it belongs

The structure is pure op: one banded unit repeated edge to edge, with checks where the fields meet. The brown ground softens the contrast, so the vibration is weaker than in a black and white print.

The V&A’s own note makes the scope of this style explicit: black and white is the core, and colourways such as this are commercial variants.

Borrow

Tile concentric diamonds so that their corners meet and form checkerboards and X shapes between them.

For a softer op field, keep the black and replace the white with one mid-tone.
